etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English cole, from Old English col, from Proto-West Germanic *kol, from Proto-Germanic *kulą (compare West Frisian koal, Dutch kool, German Kohle, Danish kul), from *ǵwelH- (“to burn, shine”). Compare Old Irish gúal (“coal”), Lithuanian žvìlti (“to twinkle, glow”), Persian زغال (zoğâl, “live coal”), Sanskrit ज्वल् (jval, “to burn, glow”), Tocharian B śoliye (“hearth”), all from the same root.

definitions.definition: (countable) A type of coal, such as bituminous, anthracite, or lignite, and grades and varieties thereof, as a fuel commodity ready to buy and burn.
(uncountable) A black or brownish black rock formed from prehistoric plant remains, composed largely of carbon and burned as a fuel.

quote.citation: 1947 January and February, O. S. Nock, “"The Aberdonian" in Wartime”, in Railway Magazine, pages 3, 5:
quote.text: Coal-eaters they may have been, but a more willing or harder working Atlantic engine was never designed.

definitions.definition: (countable) A piece of coal used for burning (this use is less common in American English)
(countable) A glowing or charred piece of coal, wood, or other solid fuel.
(Internet slang, 4chan, soyjak.party slang) Content of low quality.
(military slang, World War I– World War II) Bombs emitting black smoke on impact.[1]
(slang, obsolete) Money.[2] [late 16th c. to early 20th c.]
(intransitive) To take on a supply of coal (usually of steam ships or locomotives).
